pages.blurb: The Sunset Strip's other bar; Radio 1's Ibiza home.

pages.blurb: San Antonio's pyramid; the water parties.

pages.blurb: Oakenfold's Balearic Thursday at Heaven.

pages.name: Godskitchen
pages.blurb: The UK's trance brand, from the Junction in Cambridge to weekly nights in Northampton from 1996, then Birmingham.

pages.name: Club Guesthouse
pages.blurb: Bucharest club begun in 2010 at Traian 42, an incubator of the city's minimal scene; it moved downtown in 2020.

pages.blurb: Heavenly Recordings' thirteen Sunday nights, 7 August to 30 October 1994, in the Albany's basement on Great Portland Street; the Dust Brothers were residents.

pages.blurb: Birmingham's hard techno night; Surgeon's residency.

pages.blurb: Fabrice Emaer's theatre-club at 8 rue du Faubourg-Montmartre, opened 1 March 1978 with Grace Jones and a door that mixed Paris on purpose.

pages.name: Manto
pages.blurb: Glass-fronted Canal Street bar opened just before Christmas 1990 by Carol Ainscow and Peter Dalton; it closed in October 2013.

pages.name: Ministry of Sound
pages.blurb: Elephant and Castle; built around the sound system, Garage-style; the superclub as brand.

pages.name: Nightingale Club
pages.blurb: Birmingham gay club begun in a Camp Hill restaurant bought for £600 in 1967 or 1968; on Kent Street since 1999.

pages.name: Ostgut
pages.blurb: Snax's permanent home in a railway depot; Panorama Bar upstairs from 2000; closed 6 January 2003 after 30 hours.

pages.name: The Paradise Club
pages.blurb: Islington; AWOL (A Way of Life), jungle's breeding ground.

pages.name: Pawnshop
pages.blurb: Three-room Da'an club with Funktion-One, opened December 2019 by the people behind Korner; closed about three months by Covid rules in 2021.

pages.name: Precious Hall
pages.blurb: Sapporo's oldest operating club by RA's 2016 account; a room inspired by David Mancuso that James Murphy cites as an inspiration for Despacio.

pages.name: The Que Club
pages.blurb: A Methodist hall: House of God, Atomic Jam, Surgeon and Regis most weeks.

pages.name: RoXY
pages.blurb: Amsterdam's house institution; burned down in 1999.

pages.name: Shelley's Laserdome
pages.blurb: Sasha's residency; the North's rave club.

pages.blurb: Chelsea warehouse club at 530 West 27th Street (1989–95) where Junior Vasquez played all-morning sets to a ballroom crowd; the building became Twilo.

pages.name: Stonewall Inn
pages.blurb: The Greenwich Village bar where dancing was allowed and whose raid on 28 June 1969 set off the riots that began the gay liberation marches.

pages.name: The End
pages.blurb: Mr. C and Layo Paskin's club in a former Post Office building at 18 West Central Street, once home to its delivery horses, designed by Layo's architect father Douglas: the booth on the floor, the system before the décor. Opened December 1995; Subterrain, Flavour, Superfreq, Trash; End Recordings; AKA next door from 1998. Closed with a 24-hour party on 24 January 2009.

pages.name: The Orbit
pages.blurb: After Dark in Morley, which brought every Detroit, Berlin and Birmingham name to a mill town.

pages.name: The Saint
pages.blurb: Bruce Mailman's members-only club in the former Fillmore East, under a planetarium dome, whose membership the AIDS epidemic emptied.

pages.name: Tresor
pages.blurb: The Wertheim vault from 13 March 1991 to 2005; the Kraftwerk power station from 2007.

pages.name: UFO
pages.blurb: West Berlin's first acid/techno basement; Interfisch, Dr. Motte, Tanith.

pages.name: vurt.
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Techno club beneath a karaoke bar in Hapjeong, founded in 2014 under the slogan Ancient Future.

pages.name: WHITE Dubai
pages.blurb: Club at Meydan run by Addmind, holding about 2,000, with a top-20 DJ Mag placing; a seated dinner venue under Covid rules by November 2020.

pages.name: Zhao Dai
pages.blurb: Beijing techno club opened in 2017; shut eight months by the 2022 lockdown, reopened December 2022.

pages.name: Arcadia
pages.blurb: Pip Rush and Bertie Cole's company, builders of the Afterburner, the 50-tonne Spider (2010) and the Dragonfly (2024) at Glastonbury.

pages.name: Boy Better Know
pages.blurb: Independent label and crew founded by brothers Skepta and Jme Adenuga in north London.

pages.name: Camp Question Mark
pages.blurb: Burning Man bass camp at 2:00 running PK Sound rigs for peak crowds of 10,000 to 15,000, by Mixmag's account.

pages.name: Distruction Boyz
pages.blurb: Durban duo Que and Goldmax, producers of Babes Wodumo's 'Wololo', makers of 'Omunye' and of the 2017 album 'Gqom Is the Future'.

pages.name: Furacão 2000
pages.blurb: Rio sound system and producer, merged from Som 2000 and Guarani 2000, behind the Tornado Muito Nervoso compilations and Gaiola das Popozudas.

pages.name: Honey Soundsystem
pages.blurb: Party crew and label founded by Jacob Sperber and Ken Woodard, curators of Patrick Cowley's archive and of Tea With Honey and Deviants.

pages.name: Jazar Crew
pages.blurb: Haifa collective of five friends, throwing parties from 2011, who played Boiler Room's first Palestine broadcast in 2018.

pages.name: SFX Entertainment / LiveStyle
pages.blurb: Robert Sillerman's dance-event roll-up, bankrupt in 2016 and renamed LiveStyle; sold ID&T to Superstruct in 2021.

pages.name: Mayan Warrior
pages.blurb: Pablo González Vargas's Mexico City art car, at Burning Man from 2012; destroyed by fire in 2023 and rebuilt for 2024.

pages.name: Opulent Temple
pages.blurb: Burning Man sound camp from 2003, with a flame-throwing DJ booth; its big-name guests were not paid, Syd Gris said in 2014.

pages.name: Pxssy Palace
pages.blurb: London queer collective known for tiered ticketing, a trained support team and calling its spaces 'intentional' rather than 'safe'.

pages.name: Robot Heart
pages.blurb: Art car built on a 1972 Leland double-decker bus, on the playa since 2008; its camp numbered 90 to 100 people in 2024.

pages.name: SIREN
pages.blurb: Five-member London collective running parties, a zine, workshops and an online platform for marginalised people in nightlife.

pages.name: SubDub
pages.blurb: Leeds bass night with Iration Steppas as resident system; its crew put together the first Outlook festival in 2008.

pages.name: The Carry Nation
pages.blurb: Party formed by Will Automagic and Nita Aviance, named for the temperance campaigner; a monthly at Good Room in Brooklyn.

pages.name: WAIFU
pages.blurb: Queer and femme collective formed in 2019 after a trans woman was refused entry to a Ni-chōme party.

pages.name: Adonis
pages.blurb: Queer rave started by Shay Malt in Tottenham, with Hannah Holland and Grace Sands as residents and a vibe-based door.

pages.name: AVA Festival
pages.blurb: Sarah McBriar's Audio Visual Arts festival in Belfast, begun as a one-day event in 2014; Titanic Slipways in 2026.

pages.name: Back to the Future
pages.blurb: Dave Roberts's 1989 party series, run alongside Sunrise: grain silos in Hampshire that April, then a joint festival with Sunrise at Longwick in August.

pages.blurb: Police against the Peace Convoy on the way to Stonehenge, just over the border in Hampshire; the free festival's original wound.

pages.name: Big Day Out
pages.blurb: Ken West and Vivian Lees's touring festival, whose Boiler Room was its dance stage from 1994.

pages.name: The Blackburn raves
pages.blurb: Warehouse parties of thousands every weekend, until the police broke them in 1990.

pages.name: Boomtown
pages.blurb: Theatrical festival at the Matterley Estate since 2011, about 76,000 in 2025, permitted until 2030.

pages.blurb: The Liverpool promoters' summer night at Amnesia from 1995, on Thursdays in later years, until RA reported its departure after 22 years in 2018.

pages.name: Daisy Chain
pages.blurb: One of the nights Andrew Czezowski and Susan Carrington created at the Fridge in Brixton, running from 1987 to 1990.

pages.blurb: Desert electronic festival in southern Jordan, 2003 to 2010, that drew several thousand before apparently foundering on permits (taz).

pages.name: Dreamscape
pages.blurb: The Sanctuary; the tape packs every teenager owned.

pages.name: Duckie
pages.blurb: Club and cabaret night founded in 1995 by Simon Casson and friends; at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern until 2022, then the Eagle.

pages.blurb: Insomniac and Madison House's woodland festival at Rothbury, Michigan, grown from the Rothbury Festival of 2008.

pages.name: Sun and Bass

pages.blurb: Erol Alkan's Monday night at The End, indie into electro, the night that made his name.

pages.blurb: Denon DJ's standalone players and mixers from NAMM 2017 (SC5000 Prime, $1,899), with streaming from 2020 and stems from 2024.

pages.name: Martin Roboscan 1004
pages.blurb: Scanner from the Danish fog-machine maker Martin, introduced in September 1989 and built for the discotheque market.

pages.name: MWM Phase

pages.name: Numark NS7
pages.blurb: Controller with motor-driven seven-inch vinyl platters, shown at winter NAMM 2008 for Serato Itch.

pages.name: Pioneer DMP-555
pages.blurb: Short-lived deck that played MP3s from SD cards and had, by Pioneer's account, its first sync button; made for one year and eight months.

pages.name: Pure Data
pages.blurb: Miller Puckette's free, open-source patching environment, continuing the tradition of Max.

pages.name: Native Instruments Generator / Reaktor
pages.blurb: A modular environment for building instruments and effects; Generator was shown in 1996 and became Reaktor 2.0 in 1999.

pages.name: Richard Long's DJ crossover (RLA X3000A)

pages.name: Serato Scratch Live
pages.blurb: Timecode-vinyl DJ system from Serato, sold with Rane's USB interfaces from 2004; worked only with Rane hardware.

pages.name: fabric's Room One floor

pages.name: Steinberg Pro-24
pages.blurb: Werner Kracht's 24-channel MIDI sequencer for the Atari ST, the forerunner of Cubase.

pages.name: LennarDigital Sylenth1
pages.blurb: A CPU-light virtual analogue synth that Dance Music Northwest called the first pick of trance and EDM producers in 2017.

pages.name: Technics SL-1200MK7
pages.blurb: DJ turntable of 2019 with a coreless direct-drive motor and reverse play, following the SL-1200G revival of 2016.

pages.name: Roland TR-606 Drumatix

pages.blurb: DJ mixer — Allen & Heath's four-band, twin-filter mixer (2003), grown from Richie Hawtin's MIDI-modded Xone:62; the techno booth standard before his Model 1.

pages.name: Ibiza Uncovered
pages.blurb: Sky One's 1997 documentary series on young Britons in San Antonio; it began the Uncovered franchise (to 2002) and the Brits-abroad TV template.

pages.name: The tabloids and acid house, 1988–89
pages.blurb: How the Sun went from selling smiley T-shirts in October 1988 to 'Evils of Ecstasy' a week later, and led the press campaign against the raves until 1990.

pages.name: Eternity
pages.blurb: The hardcore and happy hardcore magazine, the rave scene reporting on itself after the press moved on.

pages.name: Groove
pages.blurb: Founded as a fanzine by DJ T. in 1989, edited in Frankfurt and from 2000 in Berlin; print until 2018, online since, run by its writers from 2024.

pages.name: Muzik
pages.blurb: IPC's dance monthly: the Muzik Awards, the serious long reads of the superclub years.

pages.name: The Wire
pages.blurb: The experimental monthly that took techno seriously as music in the 1990s; Kodwo Eshun and Simon Reynolds's writing.

pages.name: A-1 Record Shop

pages.name: Boogie Times
pages.blurb: Romford: Danny Donnelly's shop and Suburban Base label, hardcore and jungle's Essex end.

pages.name: Crazy Beat Records
pages.blurb: Upminster shop at 87 Corbets Tey Road, open almost forty years, with classic house and UK garage among its biggest sellers.

pages.name: Disk Union (Shibuya Club Music Shop)
pages.blurb: The Tokyo chain's club floor in the Antenna 21 building, Udagawacho, with more than 25,000 hip hop, house and techno records.

pages.name: Flashback Records
pages.blurb: Second-hand chain that began on Essex Road, Islington, and added Crouch End in 2006 and Shoreditch in 2014.

pages.name: Hard Wax
pages.blurb: Mark Ernestus's Berlin shop, in Kreuzberg until 2023 and in Mitte since: Basic Channel's counter, the source of Berlin's techno and dub taste, still open.

pages.name: Juno Records
pages.blurb: The online shop that replaced the counter for most of the world, with the distributor-sized catalogue of the 2000s.

pages.name: Lucky Spin
pages.blurb: Jungle shop and label: King's Road, then Holloway Road from 1994; DJ Trace and Harmony worked its counter.

pages.name: Phonica
pages.blurb: Poland Street, Soho: the dance shop of the 2000s and 2010s, still open where Black Market and the rest closed.

pages.name: Record Time
pages.blurb: Roseville, Michigan: the back room where Detroit's second wave bought their imports; Plus 8 and Transmat in the racks.

pages.name: Rounder Records
pages.blurb: Brighton Square shop and ticket outlet where Norman Cook and Skint's Damian Harris both worked; it closed on 29 July 2012.

pages.name: Selectadisc
pages.blurb: Brian Selby's Nottingham shop, where Graeme Park bought the singles; it began on Mansfield market and closed on Market Street.

pages.name: Swag Records
pages.blurb: Croydon shop run by Liz Edwards, with Terry Francis behind the counter, credited by him with the name tech-house.

pages.name: Vinyl Dreams (593 Haight Street)
pages.blurb: Mike Battaglia's dance shop at 593 Haight Street, the below-ground space that was Tweekin Records in the 1990s and 2000s.

pages.name: PK Sound
pages.blurb: Loudspeaker maker founded by Jeremy Bridge and Eroca Colins, directors of Shambhala's Village stage, whose rigs ran all but one of its main stages, by EDM Maniac's account.

pages.name: Black Moon Sound System
pages.blurb: Derbyshire free-party system whose rig was seized near Corby in July 1995 and forfeited in 1996, the first under the 1994 Act by SQUALL's account.

pages.name: Court Acoustics
pages.blurb: Stephen Court's loudspeaker firm of 1973: studio monitors, rock PAs and the Black Box rig that ran Glastonbury's NME Stage in 1994.

pages.name: Sir Coxsone's Downbeat
pages.blurb: Clement Dodd's Kingston sound, stocked with American rhythm and blues from 1953, the root of Studio One.

pages.name: Jah Shaka Sound System
pages.blurb: Neville Powell's south-east London roots reggae sound, 1970–2023: home-made sirens, dubplates and sub-bass that jungle and dubstep DJs later cited.

pages.name: The Levan horn
pages.blurb: Richard Long's sub-bass horn for the Paradise Garage: two 500-watt 18-inch drivers, a 28-square-foot mouth, rated to 30 Hz.

pages.name: Phazon
pages.blurb: New York design and installation company of which Steve Dash was a principal, maker of the PDS subs; systems for Twilo, Vinyl, Cream, Home and crobar.

pages.name: Skan PA
pages.blurb: Hire company that has run Glastonbury's second stage since 1991, with a Court Black Box rig in 1994 and Turbosound Floodlight stock by 1995.

pages.name: Tom the Great Sebastian
pages.blurb: Tom Wong's Kingston sound, from 1950, with Count Machuki on the microphone and Duke Vin selecting.

pages.name: Centreforce 88.3
pages.blurb: East London's seven-day rave station of 1989, by its own claim the first; raided and back on air through the year.

pages.name: Dream FM (Leeds)
pages.blurb: Leeds pirate station where Rachel Fox presented as Daisy & Havoc and a good share of the DJs were women.

pages.name: Kool FM
pages.blurb: The jungle station; Hype, Brockie, Eastman.

pages.name: The Breezeblock
pages.blurb: Mary Anne Hobbs's BBC Radio 1 programme of experimental electronic music, begun on 17 February 1997 and renamed in 2006.

pages.name: YFM
pages.skip: generic name and no city: the relevance rule cannot pass
pages.blurb: Johannesburg youth radio station, on air from 1997 with a less-talk, more-tunes format, that rode the wave of kwaito and house.
